Learn more at n-able.com/products/cove-data-protection. Contributed by N-able.

item.title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
item.description: SPONSORED POST: As cyberattacks become more sophisticated, organizations need to look beyond prevention and ensure they can recover critical data quickly and reliably
item.content:encoded: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. Sponsored by Infinidat

item.title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
item.description: Parliamentary committee says tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety
item.content:encoded: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology. "AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear." MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases. Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®

item.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
item.description: Attackers can crash the JVM or achieve unauthenticated RCE
item.content:encoded: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November, which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938, which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning. The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw, says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. Akamai’s Chief Information Security Architect Jan Schaumann, writing on the Openwall project’s mailing list, expressed a little discomfort with Calif’s work. “Calif.io set their priorities on publicity-maxxing, it seems,” he wrote, pointing out that the flaw-finding firm’s announcement of Java4Shell opens by stating “After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.” Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.” That second sentence perhaps supports Calif’s assertion that news of the flaw leaked before disclosure. The rest of Big Red’s flaws Java4Shell deserves a place high up on patch priority lists. So do the six 10.10 flaws Oracle reported, three in its Access Manager product, one in the Oracle Platform Security for Java, another in the WebLogic Server, and one in Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition. Big Red also repaired five 9.9-rated bugs, in Oracle Text, Hyperion, RDBMS, and Autovue. The November patch dump also includes 28 flaws rated 9.8/10. By Tenable Security’s count, 249 of the patches are for high severity bugs. Oracle’s Hyperion enterprise performance management accounts for 267 of the bugs. Such is life in the age of AI-powered flaw finders – which Calif says burned through just $200 worth of tokens to find Java4Shell. ®

item.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
item.description: NSA, Apple add to a week of high-profile network outages, largely attributed to 'routine maintenance'
item.content:encoded: Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal. A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support. A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order grounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday. Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July. Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services. A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure, riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue. “As someone who started out as a hacker, I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures. “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfortable reality I think we're grappling with is that attackers don't always have to break our systems. Sometimes, our systems are already capable of breaking on their own.” For people who couldn’t withdraw money from their bank, board a flight, or use email at work on Friday, “the disruption was real regardless of the cause,” she said. “Cybersecurity has spent decades investing in detecting threats, identifying vulnerabilities, and generating reports,” according to Kollender. “Yet we still allow for these preventable weaknesses and configurations that can bring entire systems down.” Cynthia Kaiser, senior VP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, told The Reg that the recent disruptions show “how deeply interconnected our digital infrastructure has become, and how a single technical failure or software update can cascade with outsized effects across critical systems.” AI has entered the chat Then we go and add AI to this already delicate balance, and everything essentially blows up. AI-assisted bug hunting and exploit development has surfaced more than 100,000 CVEs so far this year, with Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday disclosing more than 1,000 vulnerabilities in each of the past two months. AI has also shrunk the elapsed time between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits. “We are in an era where AI is accelerating the discovery of legacy software flaws, forcing organizations to race to patch vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them, which inevitably creates friction and disruptions,” Kaiser said. “Even when an outage isn’t caused by a cyberattack, these moments of operational distraction leave dangerous gaps open for threat actors and opportunists to take advantage of, making it crucial for both institutions and everyday individuals to remain on high alert against social engineering and unsolicited outreach.” Even when attackers aren’t using AI to facilitate intrusions, the technology itself has become a source of risk to organizations. “Autonomous agents can execute actions, change configurations, access sensitive information, and interact with critical systems at machine speed,” Kollender said. “When those systems lack proper governance and safeguards, a mistake can develop just as quickly as an attack. Former US Department of Defense network exploitation and vulnerability analyst Mike Wiacek, when asked if these regular system outages are the new normal, told us: “The brutal truth is yes. Especially in the AI world that we live in.” After the DoD, Wiacek founded Google’s Threat Analysis Group. He's since founded Stairwell, a threat-intel firm he serves as chief technology officer. “The idea that we are going to patch ourselves to security is, dare I say, an antiquated concept,” he told The Register. One of Stairwell’s engineers was doing regular, daily software development tasks on an open source library with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, and the model told the engineer about a buffer-overflow vulnerability in the code. “We weren't even looking for it,” Wiacek said. “It found a vulnerability in open source software by accident. You used to need specialized bug hunters and really, really technical security folks to discover and develop vulnerabilities and exploits. Now, it’s almost too easy to do it.” This new reality, he said, necessitates a total rethink of how we build and maintain digital infrastructure. “How do we get to a world where we assume compromised by default, and continuously recompromised, and then develop the architectures and the systems necessary to make what was the expense of incident-response investigation really fast and cheap? Because we will not be able to patch our way out of it.” It requires vulnerability managers and system administrators to patch as soon as software updates become available. But from an engineering perspective, it also means building in “as many fail-safes as possible,” Wiacek said. “An elevator doesn't have just one cable hoisting it,” he continued. “There's a lot of redundancy in those systems. Enterprises and organizations and governments haven't really had to operate like that. But that's going to be the new norm, whether we want it to be or not. Pandora's box is opened, and it's not going to go back inside.” ®

item.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
item.description: If you design a test to find misalignment, you will find misalignment
item.content:encoded: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face. Google did not respond to The Register's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255, a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says. In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident, Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test. In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said. Next time: kill switches at the ready A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check. Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website. They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall. In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests. At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments. Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.” However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register. Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.” Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ® Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.

item.title: Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take off with license data of Uber drivers
item.description: Ride-hailing biz says stolen credentials allowed crooks to help themselves to driver's license data
item.content:encoded: Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week. According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7. Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off. The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier. Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed. Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission. Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised. The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed. Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear. Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up. This isn't Uber's first brush with cybercriminals in recent months. In August, the ride-hailing giant's logistics arm, Uber Freight, confirmed a break-in after the Helix extortion crew claimed to have made off with almost a million files, including data pilfered from mailboxes and OneDrive accounts. ®

item.title: Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open
item.description: Intune feature blocks normal sign-ins without wiping data, while another test build drops Offline Maps settings
item.content:encoded: A new experimental Windows 11 build previews security features including an Intune-controlled Remote Lock, while a beta build clears away another relic from the halcyon days of Windows Phone. The security changes include viewing and individually removing passkeys stored on FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security keys, plus a preview of the Microsoft Pluton Cryptographic Provider. For enterprise administrators, though, Remote Lock is the main attraction. Finding a lost Windows device has been around for years, and you can also remotely wipe a device to prevent data from falling into the wrong hands. Remote Lock lets an administrator lock a managed device through Intune without wiping it. The instruction takes effect at the device's next check-in. Windows signs out of every active session, hides every sign-in option, and shows a locked screen. The lock survives restarts and the device going offline – only an administrator can lift it remotely. Microsoft's documentation spells out the restriction: "There is no offline or local unlock. No PIN, password, local admin, or web sign-in works on a locked device; unlock arrives only through Intune." Once the lock is applied, even stolen credentials won't restore access through the normal sign-in screen. The user's account itself is not affected; this applies only to the specific device. Though still in preview, the feature will allow IT teams to respond non-destructively to a report of a missing device. It doesn't erase data or isolate the device from the network (Microsoft directs admins to other Intune controls if that is required). The lock doesn't block Safe Mode, Windows Recovery Environment, or booting from external media. Microsoft advises keeping BitLocker enabled to protect the data. Now for the beta build, where Microsoft, in time-honored fashion, gives and takes away. The latest Windows Insider build hammers another nail into the coffin of Microsoft Maps. The Maps app was removed from the Microsoft Store and made nonfunctional in July 2025. Now Offline Maps settings are following it out, as Microsoft retires the Windows UWP Map control and Windows Maps platform APIs. The original Maps app dates back to Windows Phone 7 and appeared on the desktop with Windows 8. It continued through subsequent versions before Microsoft stopped preinstalling it with Windows 11 version 24H2. For those with a nostalgic streak, it's another piece of Windows Phone disappearing off the map. ®

item.title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
item.description: Even strict authentication mode has a hole, we're told, while basic exploit defenses are missing from the firmware
item.content:encoded: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote. Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree." He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery." He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)." Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too. He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort." Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter. He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features. "In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer. "Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid." Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching. He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase. "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure." The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available. Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables. "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said. "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled." The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply. Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell. It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

item.title: Opinion pollster Ipsos 'fesses up to 'cybersecurity incident'
item.description: Market research company brings in external specialists to grok cause and scope
item.content:encoded: Market research giant Ipsos says it's currently investigating a "cybersecurity incident," and has reported the matter to the authorities. In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal investigation is ongoing. "Upon discovery, we promptly activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident, and engaged external cybersecurity specialists to support our investigation," it said [PDF]. "The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident. We have reported the matter to the relevant authorities." Ipsos confirmed the attack had no impact on its operations or customer service delivery, however, it did not comment on the nature of the attack or whether any data was compromised. "We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously," Ipsos added. "Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly. "As the investigation is ongoing, we are not in a position to comment further at this stage." The company declined our requests for additional data, as it does not want to release unverified information to the market. Founded in France in 1975, Ipsos is one of the leading market research companies in the world, employing nearly 20,000 people and operating in 220 cities across 90 markets. It is routinely engaged by businesses for its market research data, as well as by public sector organizations for its opinion polling, often responsible for providing data regarding political views and satisfaction surveys. Tasked with procuring a wealth of data on myriad topics, Ipsos also offers data analytics services that turn the information it gathers through research, polls, and surveys into insights that inform organizations' business strategies. ®

item.title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security
item.description: Attackers try logging in to Earth’s ninth most powerful machine after status page hack exposed credentials
item.content:encoded: The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds, telcos, retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ®

item.title: Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach
item.description: The company is investigating
item.content:encoded: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data. "Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register. According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. The Register will update this story as we learn more about the breach.®

item.title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
item.description: Critical orgs around the globe under seige
item.content:encoded: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.” The FBI weighs in The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants. After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October. However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI. The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert. These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

item.title: ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years
item.description: People never learn
item.content:encoded: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®
